case_name: Ram Nath Mahto v State of Bihar
respondent:
State of Bihar
Supreme Court of India

10 April 1996
Cr.A. No. 225 of 1987 (From the Judgment and Order Dt. 17 February 1987 of the Patna High Court in Cr. A. No. 25 of 1985)
The Order of the Court was as follows :
1.  The conviction of the appellant under Section 396 IPC initially visited him with a life sentence, as ordered by the Court of Session, but on appeal to the High Court, it was reduced to ten years' rigorous imprisonment.
2.  It was a night robbery in a running train. The appellant was allegedly one of the dacoits. A person was killed during the course of commission of dacoity and the dacoits caused hurts to
facts: The Order of the Court was as follows :
It was a night robbery in a running train.
P.W.6, Diwakar Yadav, was one such person who was robbed.
The Train Ticket Examiner, P.W.3, was also one of the occupants in the train who was injured.
The occurrence took place shortly after the train left Keshar station for its onward journey to Calcutta.
This incident happened in the State of Bihar.
P.W.7 fully supported the prosecution case, deposing that P.W.6 had before him identified the appellant as the dacoit carrying a revolver.
P.W.6, however, chose not to identify the appellant at the trial and rather said that he could not recognize the accused whom he had identified at the indentification parade.
When his pointed attention was drawn towards the appellant, he did not identify him.
The trial judge recorded his remarks as to his demeanor that the witness perhaps was afraid of the accused.
It thus became evident that the witness was frightened to accord recognition to the appellant at the trial.

Despite such bend in the prosecution case, the trial court as also the High Court relied on the statement of the Magistrate, P.W.7 as to P.W.6 having identified the appellant before him at the identification parade and held the prosecution case proved beyond doubt.
Added thereto was the remark of the trial court about the demeanor of the witness P.W.6.
issues: What is the significance of evidence from an identification parade?
petitioner_arguments: The evidence of identification parade does not constitute by itself substantive evidence which is governed essentially by the provisions of Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
This Court took the view that on the facts established, the Test Identification Parade could not be considered to provide safe and trustworthy evidence on which conviction could be sustained.
respondent_arguments: The courts below relied on the statement of the Magistrate, P.W.7 as to P.W.6 having identified the appellant before him at the identification parade and held the prosecution case proved beyond doubt.
The trial court as also the High Court believed the word of P.W.7 In the context.
court_reasoning: On the facts established, the Test Identification Parade could not be considered to provide safe and trustworthy evidence on which conviction could be sustained.

The evidence of the Magistrate, P.W.7 to support the prosecution evidence to that he conducted the identification parade and before him P.W.6 had correctly identified Ram Nath to be one of the dacoits.
And the word of P.W.7 In the context has been believed by the courts below.
holding: The appeal therefore fails and is hereby dismissed.
The appellant is on bail. He shall surrender to his bail bonds.
